Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that put my body under stress

Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person

issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, carrying a weapon is hard to reconcile clinically with the indexed trauma and the rest of the profile. It implies danger from interpersonal or environmental attack rather than illness-related threat, with no supporting triggers, memory, or appraisal content indicating assault-related fear.

issues.item: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: Scanning for exits and being unable to believe reassurance about safety can occur in severe PTSD, but together they suggest a persistent external attack/escape-based threat style that fits poorly with a life-threatening illness trauma unless there is clear accompanying illness-specific danger content. No such illness-linked threat items are present.

issues.item: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
issues.explanation: The profile is clinically incoherent because it omits Triggers and Memory entirely despite an extreme PTSD severity (PCL-5=73) and instead concentrates on severe Threat, Negative Appraisals, and Maladaptive Strategies without any plausible illness-linked intrusion or cue structure.

issues.item: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
issues.explanation: Within Maladaptive Strategies, 'Avoid Circumstances ... (eg, being in the dark)' is poorly matched to a life-threatening illness trauma and points toward an assault/accident-type fear context rather than medical trauma; this clashes with 'Avoid Medical Cues' which is the trauma-congruent avoidance item.

issues.item: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: 'Dissociate Deliberately' is possible in PTSD, but paired here with strongly illness-specific avoidance and no memory/trigger content, it suggests a different symptom profile and lacks support from the stated formulation, which centers Threat–Appraisal–Strategy cycling rather than dissociative disengagement.

issues.item: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategy item 'Avoid Circumstances ... (eg, being in the dark)' is not well aligned with the trauma type of life-threatening illness. The example implies a threat context more typical of assault/accident trauma, while the rest of the profile centers on medical cues.

issues.item: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Within Maladaptive Strategies, 'Avoid Medical Cues' and 'Avoid Thinking' fit illness trauma, but 'Avoid Circumstances ... being in the dark' pulls toward a different trauma context, reducing within-node coherence.

issues.item: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
issues.explanation: Cross-node coherence is weakened because the threat items emphasize generalized danger and delays, while the negative appraisals are purely global self-defectiveness/weakness with no illness-related or health-related meaning. For life-threatening illness, some link is expected between medical threat and appraisals; these items instead suggest a different or more diffuse formulation.

vignette: David Nguyen’s life fractured when his pancreatitis turned septic, plunging him into a sudden, violent collapse that demanded immediate intubation and emergency surgery. The sterile beep of monitors, the clinical pressure of strangers working in rapid succession, and the helplessness of lying paralyzed on a gurney became etched into his nervous system. As he clawed his way back from weeks in the ICU, David began to experience a profound internal shift. He felt a deep, structural fracture, convinced there was something fundamentally wrong with him as a person. What frightened him most was the realization that he had survived only by the grace of others, cementing his belief that he was inherently weak. This sense of being broken was not passive; it actively pushed him away from the very places and thoughts that could have helped. Because he viewed himself as defective and emotionally hollow, he systematically retreated from medical settings, stopped thinking about the ordeal, and began dodging any situation that taxed his body. This avoidance was a direct refuge from the self he now despised. Within months, David’s hypervigilance became his baseline. His body sat on constant alert, muscles coiled and breathing shallow, as if the sepsis could return without warning. Even when his wife gently assured him he was healing, he found it impossible to believe the reassurance, his nervous system dismissing comfort as temporary. This distrust of safety fused with his trauma, shaping how he interpreted everyday moments. When a software deployment for his UX design firm stalled, or when a grocery checkout line moved sluggishly, he assumed something terrible was unfolding. His threat monitoring sharpened, interpreting uncertainty as imminent danger, and that fear rapidly fed back into his self-view. The longer the wait felt, the more convinced he became that he was fragile and incapable, reinforcing his negative appraisals. He came to see his own hypervigilance not as a response to trauma, but as proof of his weakness. His role as a UX designer brought these cycles into sharp relief. During a late-night usability test at his desk, a prototype for a cardiac monitoring app began lagging. The screen froze, and as the loading spinner rotated, David’s breath hitched and his shoulders locked. He was certain the delay meant a system crash, that the same catastrophic failure was happening again. Because he perceived the waiting as an immediate threat, he found himself unable to tolerate the mounting tension, which drove him to abruptly close the laptop and leave his workstation. His avoidance of physical exertion and medical interfaces had been intended to keep him safe, but the strategy only starved his nervous system of corrective experiences. Without exposure to manageable stress, his body grew more reactive, and his distrust of safety deepened. He found himself skipping morning runs and refusing to schedule routine blood work, believing that pushing himself would trigger the collapse he feared. The more he retreated, the more his physiological alarms rang, convincing him that the world was inherently unsafe and that he was ill-equipped to navigate it. Over the past year, these patterns have woven into a rigid rhythm. David’s emotional numbness has made intimacy feel distant, leaving him isolated in his own marriage despite his wife’s patience. He has come to believe that his body is a traitor, constantly signaling danger where none exists, and that his inability to relax is evidence of a broken constitution. At thirty-five, the cumulative weight of sleepless nights, avoided appointments, and constant muscle tightness finally became unsustainable. He sought therapy not because he wanted to relive the illness, but because the loop had become suffocating. He fears that if he ever stops managing his environment with meticulous care, the collapse will return. What he hopes for is not a return to who he was, but a way to sit with uncertainty without feeling his own chest tighten, to trust that a delayed response might simply be a delay, rather than a death sentence. He is ready to stop running from his own mind.
